GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: A circle touches a triangle's base, the line from the top corner to a point on the base, and the circle around the triangle; its two touch points line up with the triangle's centre.
How to play: Drag the dots A, B, C and D, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to reveal the steps of the proof one at a time.
Look for the math

Move the four dots and the little circle changes shape. Yet the line joining its two touch points keeps going through one and the same point of the triangle. This is Y. Sawayama's Lemma, the key to Thébault's problem.

One circle, three touches

Draw triangle ABC and its circumcircle. Through A draw a line meeting the base BC at D. The blue circle has its centre P on the angle bisector at D, so it touches AD at F and CD at E at the same distance. It also touches the circumcircle at K. The page's claim is that the chord EF passes through the incenter I of ABC. The logic test checks this for 261 configurations, and it held to floating-point precision.

The first two steps

Let M and N be the other places where the lines KE and KF meet the circumcircle. Because the two circles are homothetic at K, the chords MN and EF are parallel. The point M is the midpoint of the arc BC away from K, so AM bisects the angle at A and contains I. If J = AM ∩ EF, then A, F, J and K lie on one circle. Tick Step 1 and Step 2 to see these lines and circles.

Why J is the incenter

Miquel's Pivot Theorem applied to triangle AFJ says that the circle through E, J and K touches AJ at J. Now take the circle centred at M with radius MB: it passes through I and is orthogonal to the blue circle. Since ∠BKE = ∠MAC = ∠MBE, the circle through B, K and E touches BM at B. It follows that MB = MJ, and as also MB = MI, we get J = I. The status line says each of these in words as you tick Step 3 and Step 4.

What the test found

The page you can visit today puts a GeoGebra model in place of Bogomolny's Java applet, but its statement of the lemma is the same. This port follows the Java construction: a quadratic gives the blue circle's centre, then two line–circle intersections give M and N. Three harmless quirks stay: the original computes one distance it never uses, chooses between two circle hits by a one-pixel test, and averages three distances when one would do. No claim on the page failed the test; the count of 261 includes the applet's own opening picture.

Try ticking All steps and then drag D slowly along BC: watch the chord EF keep passing through the green incenter dot while every circle moves.
